title: A neurocognitive study of the emotional impact of geometrical criteria of architectural space
research_question: What is the effect of geometry of space on emotional reactivity, and how does it connect to human emotions?

participants.description: 112 participants (45 male, 67 female) including designers (Ds, n=12, mean age 33.8, SD 5.72) and non-designers (NDs, n=100, mean age 26.24, SD 4.73). Participants declared no ADHD, visual deficits other than corrected vision, heart disease, pregnancy, vertigo or claustrophobia.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 27 virtual 3D models of architectural spaces, varying in geometrical criteria: Scale (S: Small 4m, Medium 12m, Large 36m; also dome shapes at these scales), Proportion (P: changes in ceiling height (Low, Medium, High, Very high) and width (Narrow, Standard, Wide, Very wide)), Protrusion (P: gradient from 0 (simple/symmetrical) to 4 (random directions)), and Curvature (C: gradient from 0 (orthogonal/sharp) to 4 (round/curvy)). All spaces maintained a proportion of 2w/2d/2h.

measures.instrument: Length of stay in virtual space
Pupil Labs Binocular 200 Hz eye tracking
Pupil Labs Binocular 200 Hz eye tracking
Pupil Labs Binocular 200 Hz eye tracking
Pupil Labs Binocular 200 Hz eye tracking

findings.antecedent: Virtual spaces characterized by different geometries (Protrusion, Curvature, Scale, Proportion Width, Proportion Height)
findings.quote: physiological reactions of NDs towards virtual spaces (VSs) characterized by different geometries were significantly stronger than those of Ds
designers fixate significantly longer in the space observation

findings.consequent: Correlation between physiological measures and human-centred operational measures (PIS, LS)
findings.quote: No evidence was found of correlation between the physiological measures and other human-centred operational measures
Large VSs showed significantly higher PIS measurement compared with small ones
High LS was evident in both groups of participants regarding large VSs.
These VSs produced significantly larger pupillary diameter measurements
They also produced significantly fewer and shorter fixations

findings.consequent: Presence in Seconds (PIS) and Pupillary Diameter (PD)
findings.quote: Small VSs were correlated with low PIS, compared with high VSs, as well as smaller PD.
The more extreme the proportion, the stronger was the recognized measured response.
Longer PIS was measured in high VSs, compared with PIS in low VSs.
Ds, in contradiction to NDs, tended to like the ceiling as it got higher.
Moreover, a smaller PD was recognized in high VSs, compared with low spaces.
The lower the space was, the larger the pupil dilated
Larger FR was recognized in low spaces compared with high spaces
The wider the space, the longer was the PIS which was measured.
Narrow proportions received a high percentage of low LS, with greater significance among NDs, if PIS was less than ten secs.

findings.consequent: Mean Pupil Diameter (PD) and Maximal Pupil Diameter (MPD)
findings.quote: Large PD and MPD were more recognized in narrow than in wide spaces
We also recognize a tendency to a higher beta ratio in the narrow VSs
A larger FR, parallel to the gradient change of width (W1 > W3)... as well as longer FD (W1 > W3), was noted in narrow VSs.

findings.antecedent: Virtual spaces with zero curvature (C=0) and asymmetry (P=1-4)
findings.quote: stronger the protrusion was in non-curved asymmetric VSs, the larger was the PD... The lower the curvature, the larger was the PD

findings.antecedent: Virtual spaces with zero curvature (C=0) and asymmetry (P=1-4)
findings.quote: regression tree technique used to predict a response variable using a set of predictor variables resulted in significantly high LS of Ds and NDs towards these spaces.
stronger the protrusion was in non-curved asymmetric VSs, the larger was the PD
The lower the curvature, the larger was the PD
The pupillary dilation increased significantly (according to ranked analysis) as the scale increased.
A larger MPD was evidenced in asymmetrical when compared with symmetrical spaces
Tests showed a significantly high contribution of pupillary measurements compared with other types of measurements.
The combination of criteria of high curvature (C = 4) and asymmetry (P = 1-4) showed less correlation between measures than expected
it produced positive evaluation among NDs according to previous report's questionnaires

findings.antecedent: Virtual space C4P4S2 (high curvature, high protrusion, medium scale)
findings.quote: Space C4P4S2 did, however, receive, a relatively positive use score, in that 27.1% of NDs chose a 'creative use' as most suitable for it, compared with 33.3% of the D group.

findings.mechanism: assumed to be related to an aesthetic emotional response
findings.quote: High curvature, regardless of the amount of protrusion/symmetry, also produces significantly high MGSR measurements, which are assumed to be related to an aesthetic emotional response

findings.antecedent: Virtual space C2P4S2 (medium curvature, maximal protrusion, medium scale)
findings.consequent: Pupillary Diameter (PD), Maximal Pupil Diameter (MPD), Presence in Seconds (PIS), Liking Score (LS)
findings.quote: a VS characterized by medium curvature plus maximal protrusion (C2P4S2) produced the largest PD, MPD, the highest PIS, and a high LS in both groups.

findings.mechanism: perhaps contributing a peak shift effect climax, lacking in curvature and asymmetrical amorphic spaces.
findings.quote: a sharp contour appears to trigger pupillary dilation

findings.consequent: Pupillary Diameter (PD) and Maximal Pupil Diameter (MPD) as indicators of interest
findings.quote: PD and MPD are efficient indicators for the interest produced by the sharpness (no curvature) and asymmetry (C = 0+P = 4) of the spaces

findings.consequent: Unique impact (significant differences in GSR, higher PD/MPD for sharp rectangle spaces, higher beta ratio for sphere)
findings.mechanism: We suspect these shapes... produced a unique impact, since significant differences in GSR, independent of scale, were observed. In addition to higher PD and MPD for sharp rectangle spaces, a higher ẞ ratio was recognized as we compare this measurement with that of a sphere.
findings.quote: We suspect these shapes (a complete square – COPOS2 and a complete sphere – C4P0S2) produced a unique impact

findings.consequent: Pupillary Diameter (PD) and Maximal Pupil Diameter (MPD)
findings.mechanism: indicated interest as the protrusion of the space increased.
findings.quote: Sharp VS's containing a curvature of 0 (C = 0) which were also asymmetrical, were characterized by a gradual change in PD and MPD, which indicated interest as the protrusion of the space increased.
It seems that sharpness plus asymmetry (C = 0+P = 4) are criteria responsible for positive interest, as we observe all human-centred measurable variables.

findings.mechanism: related to the absence of a peak shift affect, since curvature, when non-symmetric, lacks contour and has no visually clear 'ending'. This effect absence might possibly be related to the amount of protrusion, which is 'restrained'.
findings.quote: curved (C = 4) asymmetrical VS was not positively perceived.
The narrower the space, the more discomfort can be recognized.

findings.consequent: Distress (short dwell time, low LS, high level of arousal as recorded by EEG and GSR measurements)
findings.quote: Distress emerges based on all human-centred operational measures taken (short dwell time, low LS, high level of arousal as recorded by EEG and GSR measurements).
the narrowest space was (as opposed to the lowest perceived room height)... the more coherent and significant measure in both groups of participants.
Similar effects were noted in lower spaces... the more coherent and significant measure in both groups of participants.

findings.mechanism: high ceilings remain outside one's useful field-of-view (compared with the wide VS)
findings.quote: high ceilings remain outside one's useful field-of-view

findings.mechanism: low space is more easily perceived in our normal vision field (similarly to narrow)
findings.quote: low space is more easily perceived in our normal vision field

findings.mechanism: narrow VS is characterized by vertical lines (compared with low VS). Therefore, only those who lifted their heads could react to this dimension of height.
findings.quote: narrow VS is characterized by vertical lines
long dwell-time inside a VS correlated with large spaces
The same held true for PD, and LS (high values in large VSs)
having fewer and shorter eye movement fixations in these VSs.
The results supported the notion that participants had a positive interest in large spaces
and a negative one in small spaces.

mechanisms: The moment of completing and understanding the form is pleasant, in a sense.
Peak shift effect (Purtle 1973a, Ramachandran and Hirstein 1999).
Attention exists mainly in regions of change (Ramachandran and Hirstein 1999).
The eye creates an 'ending' for 'unfinished shapes' (Kennedy 1988).
Sharp contour appears to trigger pupillary dilation, perhaps contributing a peak shift effect climax, lacking in curvature and asymmetrical amorphic spaces.
Curvature, when non-symmetric, lacks contour and has no visually clear 'ending'. This effect absence might possibly be related to the amount of protrusion, which is 'restrained'.

High ceilings remain outside one's useful field-of-view (compared with the wide VS) and low space is more easily perceived in our normal vision field (similarly to narrow), and narrow VS is characterized by vertical lines (compared with low VS).
implementation_implications: Large symmetrical spaces affect users positively and are suitable for multitude users, attracting them to stay longer.

Architectural spaces with complexity or asymmetry (non-curved asymmetry) can be suitable for uses benefiting from this reaction, but may also be distracting and not recommended for specific task-oriented uses.
Extreme proportions have the potential to negatively influence wellbeing.
Extreme proportions could be used to design spaces that create a high level of excitement, especially for experienced users (designers, or people who experience terrifying spaces in games).
Narrow spaces should be experienced as distressing, regardless of expertise or advanced familiarity.
In symmetrical spaces, if proportions and scale (as well as other criteria such as temperature, light and colour) are not distressing, they can benefit activities of concentration and rest.

tables.description: A comparison of studies based on the intersection of neuroscience and architecture (The table is based on Bower, Tucker, and Enticott 2019; Karakas and Yildiz 2020; Azzazy et al. 2020).
A keynote geometrical criteria, describing the setup implementation and virtual space characteristics for Scale, Proportion, Protrusion, and Curvature.
Demographic variables of participants in this study, including group, gender, dominant hand, dominant eye, VR experience, and computer games experience.

limitations: Movement while exploring 3D space increases data noise which disturbs the actual perceptual or cognitive activity mapping (addressed by asking participants to be seated and move as little as possible).
Need for more research to confirm the high contribution of pupillary measurements and exclude other unnecessary factors, such as luminance (which was controlled but might need further validation).
No evidence of correlation between physiological measures and other human-centred operational measures, indicating a gap between what participants think about VSs and how they react to them.

A single criterion in each stage/examination would help produce more valid data for mapping the connection between human conscious experience and architectural space (suggesting the current multi-criteria approach might be too complex).
The effect of complex shapes of large spaces is still unknown.

environmental_features: Virtual architectural spaces with varying geometric criteria: Protrusion (convex vs. concave), Curvature (curved vs. angular), Scale (small vs. large), Proportion Width (wide vs. narrow), Proportion Height (high vs. low)
control_conditions: Neutral or baseline geometric configurations (e.g., average proportions, straight walls for curvature comparison)

mechanism_chain.description: Geometric features of architectural space are perceived, leading to cognitive appraisal (e.g., perceived spaciousness, complexity, threat), which in turn elicits specific emotional states (valence, arousal) and corresponding physiological and neurocognitive responses.

steps.to_construct: Cognitive appraisal (e.g., perceived comfort, threat, spaciousness)
Physiological reactions (e.g., SCR, HR) and Neurocognitive activity (e.g., EEG)

instruments_used.name: Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM)
instruments_used.description: Pictorial scale for self-reporting emotional state

instruments_used.name: Electroencephalography (EEG)
instruments_used.construct: Brain electrical activity related to emotional processing
instruments_used.description: Measures electrical activity in the brain via electrodes on the scalp

instruments_used.name: Skin Conductance Response (SCR)
instruments_used.description: Measures changes in electrical conductivity of the skin due to sweat gland activity

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Architectural geometrical criteria have a measurable emotional and neurocognitive impact on human observers.

stimulus_images.description: Examples of virtual architectural spaces illustrating different levels of geometric features (e.g., highly curved vs. angular rooms, high vs. low protrusion, varying scales and proportions)
